summaries.summary: A hashtag is a #-preceded alphanumeric and underscore keyphrase that categorizes daily posts on Twitter, Instagram, etc., aiding search, topic tracking, and trend discovery.
Hashtags convey emotion, sentiment, sarcasm, and named entities, but joined tokens, rare entities, abbreviations, and non-standard spellings create ambiguous interpretations and hinder comprehension.
The study aims to build efficient methods for automatically splitting a hashtag into a meaningful word sequence and lists contributions.

The new dataset has segmentation for 12,594 unique hashtags and associated tweets, surpassing the previous 1,108 hashtags, and supports pairwise ranking, neural architectures, multi-task learning, 24.6% error reduction, and a 2.6% increase on SemEval 2017 sentiment analysis.

Hashtag segmentation approaches fall into gazeteer and rule based, word boundary detection, and ranking with language model and other features categories, drawing on compound splitting and word segmentation work.
Microsoft Word Breaker is a strong baseline that uses beam search to extract INLINEFORM0 best segmentations ranked by n-gram language model probability INLINEFORM1.

The authors reimplemented Word Breaker for hashtags using a Twitter-trained language model, achieving competitive performance, and use its top INLINEFORM3 segmentations as pairwise reranking candidates.
Prior work calculated segmentation ranking scores independently, ignoring relative order among top INLINEFORM0 candidates, motivating the first pairwise ranking strategy with neural architectures.
The proposed multi-task pairwise neural ranking approach incorporates relative order among candidate segmentations and adapts to single- and multi-token hashtags without additional annotations.
Hashtag segmentation divides hashtag INLINEFORM0 into meaningful words INLINEFORM1, with INLINEFORM3 possible segmentations for INLINEFORM2 characters but only one or occasionally two correct ones.

The task becomes pairwise ranking over INLINEFORM0 candidate segmentations { INLINEFORM1 }, predicting a real number INLINEFORM2 for pairs using a gold scoring function INLINEFORM8 based on ground-truth similarity.
The paper uses Levenshtein distance, though alternatives are possible, and uses the top INLINEFORM0 segmentations from Microsoft Word Breaker as initial candidates.

The pairwise neural ranking model concatenates feature vectors for a candidate pair, feeds them to a feedforward network, and minimizes Mean Squared Error (MSE) using all possible pairs and gold scores.
INLINEFORM0 is the number of training examples.
A greedy aggregation algorithm assigns each segmentation INLINEFORM0 a single score INLINEFORM2, selects the highest-scoring INLINEFORM3, removes it, and repeats until INLINEFORM6 is empty.
The Margin Ranking (MR) Loss model learns from candidate pairs INLINEFORM0 but ranks individual candidates directly using shared feedforward networks and minimizes Margin Ranking Loss (MR).
INLINEFORM0 is the number of training samples, and Figure FIGREF11 (b) presents the model architecture.

Different features address different hashtag types: linguistic features capture named entities and multi-word patterns, Good-Turing favors known multi-word segmentations, and modified Kneser-Ney favors rare words and single-word segmentations.

A binary classifier predicts probability INLINEFORM1 that INLINEFORM2 is multi-word, uses INLINEFORM3 as adaptive gating, obtains labels from ground-truth segmentation, and is jointly trained with the pairwise ranker.

INLINEFORM0 is the adaptive gating value, INLINEFORM1 indicates whether INLINEFORM2 is multi-word, INLINEFORM3 is the number of training examples, and INLINEFORM4 and INLINEFORM5 are equal loss weights.

The segmentation feature vector INLINEFORM0 is divided into INLINEFORM1 with modified Kneser-Ney smoothing features and INLINEFORM2 with Good-Turing smoothing and linguistic features, combined by adaptive gating INLINEFORM6 before feedforward network INLINEFORM7.

The model uses summation with padding because it performs similarly to multi-column networks BIBREF29, and Figure FIGREF11 (c) shows the architecture alongside an analogue multi-task formulation for Margin Ranking loss.

Candidate segmentation features include word counts, word lengths, dictionary proportions, Google Web 1TB corpus ngram counts, trigram probabilities from Gigaword corpus and 1.1 billion English tweets from 2010, and boolean word-shape and named-entity features.

Hashtag features INLINEFORM1 include hashtag length, Google 1TB corpus ngram count, dictionary, named-entity, camel case, number-ending, consonant-only booleans, and Word Breaker best-ranked candidate features.

The PyTorch implementation uses a pairwise ranker with three eight-node hidden layers, tanh activation, one linear output, an auxiliary classifier with one eight-node hidden layer and sigmoid output, Adam, dropout of 0.5, learning rates 0.01 and 0.05, and 100 epochs.
The baseline reimplements Word Breaker BIBREF16 with a language model trained on 1.1 billion tweets using Good-Turing smoothing with SRILM BIBREF33, and sets INLINEFORM1 for all experiments.

Experiments use STAN INLINEFORM0 with 1,108 unique English hashtags from 1,268 randomly selected tweets and STAN INLINEFORM1 with all 12,594 unique English hashtags and associated tweets from the same Stanford dataset.
This section presents experimental results comparing the proposed method with other state-of-the-art approaches on hashtag segmentation datasets, followed by sentiment analysis experiments.
The pairwise neural ranker is compared with baseline and state-of-the-art approaches.
One comparison approach is the original hashtag as a single token.
A rule-based segmenter employs word-shape rules with an English dictionary BIBREF13.
A Viterbi model uses word frequencies from a book corpus BIBREF0.
The GATE Hashtag Tokenizer combines dictionaries and gazetteers in a Viterbi-like algorithm BIBREF11.
A maximum entropy classifier (MaxEnt) trained on the STAN INLINEFORM0 training dataset predicts spaces at each hashtag position and is the current state-of-the-art BIBREF14.
The authors reimplement the Word Breaker algorithm using beam search and a Twitter ngram language model BIBREF16.

A pairwise linear ranker uses the same features as the neural model, perceptron BIBREF38, hinge loss between INLINEFORM0 and a scoring function similar to INLINEFORM1, and is trained on STAN INLINEFORM2.

Evaluation uses top INLINEFORM0 ( INLINEFORM1 ) accuracy (A@1, A@2), average token-level F INLINEFORM2 score (F INLINEFORM3 @1), and mean reciprocal rank (MRR), with segmentation-level accuracy and MRR requiring full human-segmentation matches.

Tables TABREF32 and TABREF33 report STAN INLINEFORM0 and STAN INLINEFORM1 results, with pairwise neural rankers trained on 2,518 manually segmented hashtags, MSE+multitask performing best, 24.6% and 16.5% error reductions on multi-token hashtags, and remaining top-one prediction challenges.
The improved Word Breaker with a Twitter-specific language model is a strong baseline, and BIBREF14 used a 4-gram language model trained on 476 million tweets from 2009.

Table TABREF45 shows modified Kneser-Ney smoothing performs best on single-token hashtags, while Good-Turing and Linguistic features work best on multi-token hashtags, and Table TABREF47 gives qualitative analysis.

Longer hashtags with more than three tokens are harder, with MSE+multitask segmentation-level accuracy dropping to 82.1%, though close-to-correct predictions yield higher token-level F INLINEFORM0 scores.
Using smaller Twitter language models reduces F INLINEFORM0 score by only 1.4% and 3.9% with 10% and 1% of the total 1.1 billion tweets, respectively.
On 500 random English hashtags from 2019, the approach achieves segmentation-level accuracy of 94.6% and average token-level F INLINEFORM0 score of 95.6%.
The extrinsic evaluation studies the impact of the hashtag segmentation system on Twitter sentiment analysis, using the best model (MSE+multitask) under the name HashtagMaster.
The study compares BiLSTM+Lex BIBREF42 sentiment analysis under three hashtag configurations, including HashtagMaster segmentation, using settings from BIBREF42 teng-vo-zhang:2016:EMNLP2016.
The SemEval 2017 subtask A dataset is used, with 49,669 training and development tweets, 40,000 for training, and 12,284 test tweets containing 12,128 hashtags.
Table TABREF59 reports results on 3,384 tweets where HashtagMaster predicted a split, improving average recall and F INLINEFORM0 by 2% over unsegmented hashtags.

Automatic hashtag segmentation can improve text classification BIBREF13, named entity linking BIBREF10, recommendations BIBREF45, emotion analysis BIBREF46, and sarcasm and irony detection BIBREF11, BIBREF47.

The authors proposed a pairwise neural ranking model for hashtag segmention, constructed a larger curated dataset, showed state-of-the-art improvements, and demonstrated downstream sentiment analysis benefits.
